newsitem.title: INDIA: India concerned by U.S. move on Pakistan arms aid.
newsitem.headline: India concerned by U.S. move on Pakistan arms aid.

text.p: India expressed concern on Friday over a recent U.S. decision to ease curbs on military and economic aid to Pakistan, saying the move could hurt peace talks underway between the two South Asian neighbours.
"The government has been informed of an amendment to the U.S. Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, which has been passed by the Senate of the U.S. Congress," an Indian foreign ministry spokesman said.
The amendment lifts existing restrictions on Washington's military and economic aid to Pakistan that were in place due to "Pakistan's externally assisted nuclear weapons programme," he said.

"This amendment comes in the wake of reports of Pakistan having tested a medium-range missile and establishing a missile facility with Chinese assistance. These reports have serious implications for India," the spokesman said.

India and Pakistan have fought three wars since 1947. Each says it has no nuclear weapons but experts say both nations can swiftly assemble them. Pakistan tested a ballistic missile earlier this month.

Beijing and Islamabad deny reports that nuclear-armed China transferred missiles and nuclear weapons components to Pakistan. But India, wedged between the two, views their decades-old close military ties with considerable concern.
India said a similar amendment last year, which eased U.S. sanctions imposed on Pakistan in 1990 on suspicions over its nuclear programme, was a cause for concern.
"Since then there has been no let up in Pakistan's pursuit of nuclear weapons and their means of delivery," the spokesman said. "This amendment is part of an incremental process."
"It cannot but be viewed with concern in India as encouragement to Pakistan's clandestine nuclear and missile programmes," the spokesman said.
The Foreign Ministry said the amendment could damage bilateral talks between the archrivals that resumed in March after three years of tense silence.
"It will vitiate the atmosphere of the dialogue which India and Pakistan have just resumed, by emboldening elements in Pakistan who are not in favour of that process," he said without elaborating.
"The government will take appropriate steps to safeguard India's security," the spokesman added.

India has successfully tested the 250-km (150-mile) range Prithvi surface-to-surface missile and a 150-km (90-mile) variant. New Delhi denies reports that it has already deployed the ballistic missiles on its border with Pakistan but says it will deploy the Prithvi if necessary.
